title: Christ Crucified and the Wisdom the Spirit Reveals
summary: Paul reminds the Corinthians that he came to them without impressive eloquence, determined to know nothing among them but Jesus Christ crucified, so that their faith would rest on God's power. He then explains that there is a true wisdom, hidden from the rulers of this age who crucified the Lord of glory, which God has revealed by his Spirit. Only those who have the Spirit can receive it, because it is spiritually discerned, and believers have the mind of Christ.
story: Chapter 1 set the message of the cross against the wisdom of the world and showed that God chose the lowly Corinthians to shame the wise. Chapter 2 continues the argument in two steps. First, Paul turns to his own preaching as evidence: the way he came to Corinth matched the message he brought. Second, he answers an obvious objection. If the gospel looks like foolishness, is there no wisdom in it at all? There is, Paul says, but it is God's wisdom, given by the Spirit, not a higher level of human cleverness. Chapter 3 will then turn this back on the Corinthians, who claim to be spiritual but act like people of the flesh.
historical:
Paul's arrival in Corinth, around AD 50, came after a hard stretch of travel. Acts records that he had been beaten and imprisoned in Philippi, driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, and met with a mixed response in Athens (Acts 16 to 17). He came to Corinth alone at first, working as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, and Acts 18:9-10 records that the Lord spoke to him in a vision at night, telling him not to be afraid. That background helps explain his words about coming "in weakness and fear, and with much trembling".

The "rulers of this age" who crucified the Lord of glory (verse 8) are understood in different ways. Many interpreters take them as the human authorities responsible for Jesus' death, such as Pilate, Herod Antipas, and the temple leadership. Others take them as the spiritual powers standing behind human rulers, since Paul elsewhere speaks of rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms (Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 2:15). Some combine the two, seeing human rulers as agents of larger powers.
cultural:
Paul's refusal of "persuasive words of wisdom" (verse 4) went against the expectations of a city that honored rhetoric. Traveling orators often made a grand entrance, displayed their skill, and won followers and fees. Paul deliberately chose another way. He supported himself by manual labor, which many educated Greeks and Romans regarded as degrading, and he spoke plainly. The word he uses for "demonstration" (apodeixis) was a technical term in rhetoric for a compelling proof. Paul's proof was not an argument but the Spirit's power at work.

The language of mystery would also have sounded familiar. The Greek world had mystery cults, such as the rites of Eleusis near Athens, in which initiates learned secret rituals that promised a better fate after death. Paul uses similar words (mystery, mature, hidden) but gives them new content. God's mystery is not a secret rite for a spiritual elite but the plan of salvation, once hidden and now openly revealed in the crucified Christ.
literary: The chapter falls into two parts. Verses 1 to 5 are autobiographical, framed by the contrast between human wisdom and God's power. Verses 6 to 16 are an argument about true wisdom, moving from what it is not (the wisdom of this age), to what it is (God's hidden wisdom, destined for our glory), to how it is known (revealed by the Spirit), to who can receive it (the spiritual person, not the natural one). Paul builds the argument on an analogy in verse 11: only a person's own spirit knows that person's thoughts, and only God's Spirit knows God's. The quotation in verse 9 is not an exact match for any single Old Testament verse; it is closest to Isaiah 64:4 with echoes of other passages. The chapter ends with Isaiah 40:13 and a bold claim: "But we have the mind of Christ."

outline.t: Paul's preaching: Christ crucified in weakness and power
God's hidden wisdom, unknown to the rulers of this age
Revealed by the Spirit who searches the depths of God
The natural person, the spiritual person, and the mind of Christ

doctrines.note: The Spirit searches the depths of God and knows God's thoughts as a person's spirit knows his own, which implies the Spirit's divine identity. He reveals to believers what God has freely given them and enables them to understand it.

God's wisdom cannot be discovered by human searching; it has to be revealed. Paul describes a chain of revelation: God's plan, revealed by the Spirit, spoken by apostles in words taught by the Spirit, and received by those who have the Spirit.
Paul's message is Jesus Christ and him crucified. The crucifixion is the point at which the rulers of this age showed their blindness, and it is the content of God's wisdom.

words.note: Psuchikos, natural, from psuche, soul or life. It describes a person who lives only by natural human capacities, without the Spirit of God. The word does not mean bad or sinful in itself, but limited. In 15:44 Paul uses it for the natural body in contrast with the spiritual resurrection body.

Pneumatikos, spiritual, meaning shaped and enabled by the Spirit of God. The Corinthians seem to have used the word to rank themselves above others. Paul redefines it: the spiritual person is not a religious elite but anyone who has received the Spirit and so can receive God's gifts, and in chapter 3 he will say that the Corinthians are not living up to the name.

Musterion, mystery. For Paul it means something hidden in God's purpose and now revealed. In verse 1 some manuscripts read testimony (marturion) and others mystery; either way, the content is God's plan fulfilled in Christ crucified, not a secret for insiders.

Anakrino, to examine, investigate, or judge, as in a legal inquiry. It appears three times in verses 14 and 15. Spiritual things are discerned spiritually, and the spiritual person examines all things but is not subject to anyone's judgment. The Corinthians were examining and ranking their leaders, and Paul will return to this word in 4:3-4.

christ: This chapter shows Christ as the content and the key of God's wisdom. Paul's resolve to know nothing "except Jesus Christ and Him crucified" (verse 2) is not a narrowing of interest but a choice of center: everything else he teaches flows from the cross. Christ is called "the Lord of glory" (verse 8), a striking title for a crucified man, since glory in Scripture belongs to God. The rulers who crucified him did not recognize who he was. The chapter ends with the claim that believers have "the mind of Christ" (verse 16). In context this is not a promise of private knowledge but a way of thinking shaped by the crucified Lord, which Paul describes in Philippians 2:5-8 as the mind that emptied itself and humbled itself to death on a cross.
questions: Paul came in weakness and fear, yet God's power worked through him. When have you seen God work through weakness rather than impressive strength?
What is the difference between faith that rests on human wisdom and faith that rests on God's power? How would you know which one is yours?
Paul says believers have the mind of Christ. What would it look like for that to shape a decision you face this week?
